content:
In the past few days, two reports have pointed to different ways Apple can boost its profits by growing its services revenue.

In my view, Apple should absolutely pursue the first of these approaches, but not the second—and it seems Phil Schiller would agree…

Let me first summarise the two reports.

Home security and monitoring services

On Friday, a Bloomberg report said Apple may be planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, expected to debut alongside several long-awaited new home hardware products.

Squeezing more money out of the App Store

A second Bloomberg report, on Sunday, said Apple is exploring ways to squeeze more revenue and profit out of the App Store.

Apple should not adopt the latter approach

On the contrary, I believe the second approach would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly on iPhone app sales is already being questioned by regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you have to go through the official App Store—there is no alternative, and you must accept Apple's terms with zero negotiating power.

I know many people feel that nobody is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but this view doesn't align with how even the most laissez-faire capitalism actually works: even in the US, antitrust law has existed since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, you are subject to rules of conduct to ensure you don't abuse that position.

Trying to extract more money from the App Store is the opposite of "skating to where the puck is going"—and Schiller is reportedly in agreement. Bloomberg noted this is one of the reasons he stepped back from frontline work.

Innovative services are the right direction

Apple should launch brand-new, innovative services that customers are happy to pay for. I can easily see the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

As I said back in 2024, developing its own smart home cameras would be one of the smartest moves the company could make. I expressed the same view about the long-rumoured Apple smart doorbell at the time. Adding optional service bundles to security products makes perfect sense, for two reasons.

First, all the privacy reasons I've mentioned before apply. HomeKit Secure Video has already done extensive work in protecting the privacy of security camera footage. If there's any company I'd trust to run AI analysis on security camera footage, it's Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I'm convinced there are plenty of other areas where Apple could offer a similar advantage.

For me, the point is that Apple needs to treat services with the same attitude it brings to hardware—building outstanding products that customers are happy and willing to pay for, rather than making money in ways that annoy customers, developers, and regulators.

What do you think? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
